sentences.text: Mature Kambara crocodilians generally reached lengths of 3 to 4 meters and possessed a typically crocodilian skull that was roughly triangular, starting narrow at the snout and widening towards the back. They are generally considered to have been a semi-aquatic generalist with an appearance resembling modern crocodiles.

The species K. murgonensis is described as having a moderately broad snout and a robust build. The strong bite of K. taraina suggests it could hunt larger, more terrestrial prey, while older species likely fed on smaller animals.

Ralph Molnar first formally described Kambara material in 1982, initially identifying it as a Miocene crocodylid. The first remains were found in the Oakdale Sandstone Formation near Murgon, Queensland.

The name Kambara derives from an Aboriginal word for crocodile within the Queensland language group. The species K. taraina was named in 2009 by Lucas A. Buchanan, and its name derives from the Darumbal dialect, meaning crocodile.

The flattened skull shape and depositional environment suggest Kambara were semi-aquatic ambush predators. Differences in limb bones suggest Kambara may have been better adapted for walking on land than modern Australian crocodiles.

The genus Kambara was described by Willis, Molnar, and Scanlon in 1993. Four species of Kambara are known: K. murgonensis (type species, Willis et al., 1993), K. implexidens (Salisbury & Willis, 1996), K. molnari (Holt et al., 2005), and K. taraina (Buchanan, 2009). Kambara belongs to the parent group Mekosuchinae.

Kambara lived during the Eocene epoch. Kambara was an extinct Mekosuchine crocodilian that lived during the Eocene and Oligocene periods in present-day Australia. With an age of approximately 55 million years, Kambara fossils are among the oldest Tertiary fossils found in Australia. Kambara is the oldest known Mekosuchine.
Some studies suggest Kambara was not a mekosuchine, though this view is not supported by all authors.
It is debated whether Kambara was fully terrestrial or simply better adapted for land than modern crocodiles.

It is unclear how K. murgonensis and K. implexidens differed ecologically despite their anatomical differences. Researchers debate whether K. murgonensis and K. implexidens coexisted or were driven together by drought.
